What Denial Looks Like
•  Little recognition of deeper cultural differences
•  Indifference or disinterest toward cultural variation
•  Comfortable with the familiar; avoids difference
•  Does not see communication as “cultural”
•  Assumes “others are basically like me”
Your Developmental Goal
Begin to notice cultural differences — starting with observable, non-threatening differences and gradually expanding to deeper cultural patterns.

Curiosity, not judgment, is the key move.
2 / 13 1
Tutorial 1 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Understanding Your IDI Results
What Denial Means — and What It Doesn't
Why This Matters
Before any growth can occur, you need an accurate map of where you are. Denial does not mean you are a bad person — it means your awareness of deeper cultural difference is still developing.
Learner Goals
Accurately describe what the Denial orientation means on the IDI continuum
Distinguish between Developmental Orientation (DO) and Perceived Orientation (PO)
Accept your results without judgment as a starting point for growth
Developmental Activity
Journal Prompt: Write 3–5 sentences about a recent moment at work when a colleague reacted to a situation very differently than you did. What might explain that difference beyond personality?
Reflection Question
How did you feel when you first saw your IDI score? What assumptions did you have about where you would land?
Facilitator Note
Normalize the result. Only ~2% of the general population scores in Denial — but this is not a failing grade. Emphasize that self-awareness is the first and most critical step on the continuum.
3 / 13 2
Tutorial 2 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Noticing Cultural Difference
Training Your Eye to See What You've Been Missing
Why This Matters
People in Denial often don't notice deeper cultural differences (e.g., conflict resolution styles, communication norms) even when they are present. The developmental goal here is observation, not judgment.
Learner Goals
Identify at least three observable cultural differences in your daily work environment
Distinguish surface-level from deeper differences (e.g., food vs. decision-making styles)
Begin building a personal vocabulary for cultural observation
Developmental Activity
Cultural Difference Log: For one week, note one interaction per day where you observed someone responding to a situation differently than you would. Record what you saw — not what you concluded.
Reflection Question
What kinds of differences are easiest for you to notice? What might you be systematically overlooking?
Facilitator Note
Start with low-threat, observable differences. Food, holidays, and communication styles are safe entry points. Do not push immediately to race or disability — meet the learner where they are.
4 / 13 3
Tutorial 3 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Expanding Your Cultural Awareness
Moving from Disinterest to Curiosity
Why This Matters
Denial often includes an affective component: disinterest or indifference toward cultural difference. Shifting this emotional posture toward genuine curiosity is a core developmental move.
Learner Goals
Identify at least two cultural groups you know very little about
Describe what genuine curiosity (vs. tolerance) looks and feels like
Practice asking culturally curious questions in a low-stakes setting
Developmental Activity
Curiosity Interview: Identify a colleague or community member from a cultural background different from your own. Prepare three open-ended, genuinely curious questions. Conduct the conversation and write a short reflection.
Reflection Question
When you hear the word "culture," what images come to mind? What does that reveal about the breadth — or limits — of your cultural lens?
Facilitator Note
Watch for learners who intellectually endorse diversity while emotionally staying disengaged. Curiosity requires emotional activation, not just cognitive acknowledgment.
5 / 13 4
Tutorial 4 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Recognizing Cultural Lenses
Everyone Has a Cultural Worldview — Including You
Why This Matters
A defining feature of Denial is the assumption that one's own perspective is simply "the normal way." Helping learners see that their own values and behaviors are culturally shaped — not universal — is transformative.
Learner Goals
Identify at least three values or behaviors you hold that are culturally shaped
Explain what it means to have a "cultural lens"
Describe a situation where your cultural lens may have limited your understanding
Developmental Activity
Values Mapping Exercise: Review a list of workplace values (e.g., directness, punctuality, hierarchy, individualism). Rate how strongly each resonates. Then explore: where did these values come from? Who taught you these are "just how things work"?
Reflection Question
What would it mean for your professional practice if many of your "standard" ways of doing things are actually culturally specific — not universal?
Facilitator Note
Frame this as empowering, not destabilizing. Recognizing your own cultural lens is not about guilt — it is about gaining precision and flexibility.
6 / 13 5
Tutorial 5 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Cultural Difference in Disability Services
Applying Intercultural Awareness to Your Work at DSD
Why This Matters
Abstract intercultural concepts must connect to real work to stick. Disability services involves navigating race, ethnicity, socioeconomic background, disability identity, and community culture simultaneously.
Learner Goals
Name two ways cultural background shapes how people experience disability services
Identify a DSD policy or practice that may have unintended cultural limitations
Connect intercultural awareness to equitable service delivery outcomes
Developmental Activity
Case Scenario Reflection: Read an anonymized scenario of a service interaction where cultural misalignment affected the outcome. Identify: What cultural factors were at play? What was missed? What could have been done differently?
Reflection Question
How might the families and individuals you serve experience your program differently based on cultural background — even if you are trying to treat everyone the same?
Facilitator Note
This is a bridge module. Connect the IDI growth work explicitly to the One DSD equity mission. The goal is not just personal development — it is organizational transformation.
7 / 13 6
Tutorial 6 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
From Avoidance to Engagement
Interrupting the Denial Pattern in Real Time
Why This Matters
Denial includes behavioral avoidance — gravitating toward the familiar and withdrawing from difference. Recognizing this pattern in your own behavior is the first step to interrupting it.
Learner Goals
Identify your personal patterns of avoidance around cultural difference
Distinguish between comfort and growth in cross-cultural interactions
Commit to one low-stakes cross-cultural engagement this week
Developmental Activity
Avoidance Audit: List three professional or community spaces you regularly inhabit. Who is absent? Who do you rarely have substantive conversations with? What one small step could increase your cross-cultural exposure this month?
Reflection Question
What is the cost — to you, your colleagues, and the people you serve — of staying in the familiar and avoiding cultural difference?
Facilitator Note
Do not shame avoidance. Acknowledge it as a normal comfort-seeking behavior. The goal is gentle, consistent stretching — not an overwhelming plunge into discomfort.
8 / 13 7
Tutorial 7 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Learning Through Story
Using Narrative to Build Cultural Empathy
Why This Matters
Story is a developmentally appropriate tool for people in Denial. First-person narratives make abstract cultural difference concrete and human — lowering resistance and building genuine empathy.
Learner Goals
Engage with one first-person account of cultural difference from a different background
Practice perspective-taking without evaluating or comparing
Identify at least one assumption a story challenged you to reconsider
Developmental Activity
Story-Based Learning: Select one memoir, podcast episode, documentary, or oral history from a cultural group you are less familiar with. Respond: What surprised you? What challenged an assumption? What will you carry forward?
Reflection Question
What difference does it make to receive cultural experience from a first-person narrative versus a textbook or training manual?
Facilitator Note
Provide a curated list — podcasts, short films, TED talks — across multiple cultural dimensions (race, disability, immigrant experience, LGBTQ+, socioeconomic). Learners in Denial need low-barrier on-ramps.
9 / 13 8
Tutorial 8 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Understanding the Orientation Gap
Why You Thought You Were Further Along
Why This Matters
Most people in Denial significantly overestimate their intercultural competence. The Orientation Gap (PO minus DO) can be disorienting. Helping learners process it with curiosity rather than defensiveness is essential.
Learner Goals
Accurately define the Orientation Gap and explain why it exists
Describe two reasons people in Denial tend to overestimate their competence
Develop a constructive emotional response to gap awareness
Developmental Activity
Gap Reflection: Write a short response to three prompts — (1) What did you believe about your intercultural competence before the IDI? (2) Where did that belief come from? (3) How can the gap become useful information rather than a discouraging verdict?
Reflection Question
Are there situations where you assumed you were being culturally competent — but may have been operating from a narrower lens than you realized?
Facilitator Note
The gap is nearly universal. Normalizing it explicitly reduces shame and opens curiosity. "Even experienced DEI practitioners show an Orientation Gap" is a useful frame.
10 / 13 9
Tutorial 9 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Building Your Development Plan
Setting Intentional Goals for Intercultural Growth
Why This Matters
Growth on the IDI continuum is not automatic — it requires structured, intentional effort. An Intercultural Development Plan (IDP) translates awareness into action and creates accountability over time.
Learner Goals
Draft a personal IDP with at least two specific, measurable growth goals
Identify a practice or experience that will support each goal
Establish a personal check-in cadence to monitor progress
Developmental Activity
IDP Draft: (1) My primary developmental goal for the next 90 days is... (2) The specific action I will take is... (3) I will know I am making progress when... (4) My accountability partner or check-in structure is...
Reflection Question
What conditions — in your schedule, your workplace, your mindset — would support or hinder your IDP goals? What do you need to put in place now?
Facilitator Note
IDPs are most effective when tied to real, recurring work situations. Help the learner identify 2–3 specific professional moments each week where they can practice intentionally.
11 / 13 10
Tutorial 10 of 10  ·  Denial → Polarization
Moving Toward Polarization
A Developmental Bridge to the Next Orientation
Why This Matters
As awareness increases, learners will begin to notice more cultural difference — and may react with judgment or discomfort. This is Polarization emerging, and it is a sign of growth. Preparing learners for this transition prevents regression.
Learner Goals
Describe the Polarization orientation and how it differs from Denial
Explain why moving toward Polarization is a step forward, not backward
Identify early signs that your cultural awareness is developing
Developmental Activity
Continuum Mapping: Draw your own version of the IDC. Mark where you are now (Denial). Mark where you want to be in 12 months. In between, write 3–5 "bridge moments" — specific experiences or insights that will mark your movement forward.
Reflection Question
As you begin to notice more cultural difference, what emotions come up? How will you use those emotions as information rather than as a reason to withdraw or judge?
Facilitator Note
Celebrate growth explicitly, even when it feels uncomfortable. A learner who is noticing cultural differences and feeling uncertain is more developed than one who isn't noticing anything. That tension is the work.
12 / 13 Your Path Forward
From Awareness to Action — A Summary
01
Accept Results
Denial is a starting point, not a verdict. You are now aware.
02
Start Noticing
Practice observing cultural difference without evaluating it.
03
Get Curious
Shift from indifference to genuine interest in others' experiences.
04
Engage Daily
Use your IDP. Take one intentional step every week.
05
Expect Discomfort
As awareness grows, tension is progress. Stay in the work.
